title: Ch 15 · Transport Systems in Living Things

questions.q: Which are the three main parts of the human transport system?
questions.explain: The human transport system has a pump (the heart), a liquid (the blood) and tubes (the blood vessels) that carry blood around the body.
questions.lo: State the three main parts of the human transport system and the function of the heart

notes.0: Xylem and phloem are transport tissues found in plants, not in humans. The human system is made of a pump, a liquid and tubes.
notes.2: The stomach is part of the digestive system. It digests food but does not carry substances around the body.
notes.3: The lungs are part of the respiratory system, where gases are exchanged. They are not the tubes that carry blood around the body.

questions.q: What is the function of the heart?
choices: to carry oxygen in red blood cells
to pump blood around the body
questions.explain: The heart is a muscular pump. It pumps blood through the blood vessels to all parts of the body.
questions.lo: State the three main parts of the human transport system and the function of the heart

notes.0: Exchange of substances with cells happens across the thin walls of the capillaries, not in the heart.
notes.1: Oxygen is carried by red blood cells in the blood. The heart is an organ and does not carry oxygen itself.
notes.2: Food is digested in the digestive system. The heart does not make or digest food.

questions.q: The transport system is like pipes, a liquid and a pump. The pipes are the
questions.explain: Blood vessels are tubes that carry blood around the body, like pipes. Blood is the liquid and the heart is the pump.
questions.lo: State the three main parts of the human transport system and the function of the heart

notes.1: Blood is what flows through the system. In the model it matches the liquid, not the pipes.
notes.2: The lungs are part of the respiratory system. They are not one of the three parts in the pipes, liquid and pump model.
notes.3: The heart pushes blood along. In the model it matches the pump, not the pipes.

why.right: Blood vessels match pipes because they are tubes that carry blood to and from all parts of the body.
wrong: Blood vessels match pipes because they push the blood around the body with strong regular beats.
Blood vessels match pipes because they store all of the blood that the body needs in one place.

questions.q: Which part of blood transports oxygen?
questions.explain: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body.
questions.lo: State the functions of the components of blood

notes.0: White blood cells protect the body against infection. They do not carry oxygen.
notes.1: Platelets help blood to clot when a blood vessel is cut. They do not carry oxygen.
notes.3: Plasma carries dissolved food, wastes and carbon dioxide. Oxygen is carried by a type of blood cell.

questions.q: Digested food and waste products are carried dissolved in the
questions.explain: Plasma is the liquid part of blood. Digested food and waste products are dissolved in it and carried around the body.
questions.lo: State the functions of the components of blood

notes.0: White blood cells protect the body against infection. Dissolved substances are carried in the liquid part of blood.
notes.2: Red blood cells carry oxygen. Dissolved food and wastes are carried in the liquid part of blood.
notes.3: Platelets help blood to clot. Substances that are dissolved travel in the liquid part of blood, not in cell fragments.

why.right: Digested food travels in plasma because plasma is mostly water, so the food can dissolve in it.
wrong: Digested food travels in plasma because plasma is made of cells that store the food inside them.
Digested food travels in plasma because plasma flows only between the digestive system and the heart.

questions.q: Which part of blood helps to form a blood clot?
questions.explain: Platelets are cell fragments in the blood. They help blood to clot at a wound, which stops bleeding.
questions.lo: State the functions of the components of blood

notes.1: Plasma is the liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances. It is not the part that starts a clot.
notes.2: Red blood cells carry oxygen around the body. They are not the part of blood that helps a clot to form.
notes.3: White blood cells protect the body by fighting germs. They are not the part of blood that helps a clot to form.

questions.q: Which part of blood protects the body against infection?
questions.explain: White blood cells protect the body against infection by fighting germs that enter the body.
questions.lo: State the functions of the components of blood

notes.0: Plasma is the liquid part of blood that carries dissolved food and wastes. It is not the part that fights germs.
notes.1: Platelets help to form a clot that seals a wound. They do not fight the germs that cause infection.
notes.3: Red blood cells carry oxygen. They are not the cells that fight germs.

questions.q: A person cuts a finger and the bleeding soon stops. Which part of blood acted?
questions.explain: Platelets help blood to form a clot at the cut. The clot seals the wound and the bleeding stops.
questions.lo: State the functions of the components of blood

notes.0: Red blood cells carry oxygen. Bleeding stops when a clot forms, and a different part of blood helps the clot to form.
notes.1: White blood cells fight germs that may enter the cut. They do not form the clot that stops the bleeding.
notes.2: Plasma is the liquid that carries dissolved substances. Bleeding stops when a clot forms, which needs another part of blood.

why.right: The bleeding stops because platelets help the blood to form a clot that seals the cut.
wrong: The bleeding stops because white blood cells fill the cut and kill the germs there.
The bleeding stops because the heart stops pumping blood to the cut finger for a while.

questions.q: Mineral salts absorbed in the large intestine are carried in the
questions.explain: Mineral salts dissolve in the plasma, the liquid part of blood, and are carried around the body.
questions.lo: State the functions of the components of blood

notes.0: Red blood cells carry oxygen. Dissolved substances such as mineral salts travel in the liquid part of blood.
notes.1: Platelets help blood to clot. Substances absorbed from the intestine are dissolved and carried in the liquid part of blood.
notes.3: White blood cells fight infection. Substances absorbed from the intestine are dissolved and carried in the liquid part of blood.

why.right: Mineral salts travel in plasma because they dissolve in the water that makes up most of plasma.
wrong: Mineral salts travel in plasma because plasma is made of cells that store mineral salts.
Mineral salts travel in plasma because plasma flows only between the intestines and the heart.

questions.q: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the organs and tissues of the body.
questions.lo: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries

notes.0: Veins carry blood in the other direction, back to the heart. Think about which vessel blood enters first when the heart pumps.
notes.1: Xylem is a transport tissue in plants. It is not a blood vessel.
notes.2: Capillaries are tiny vessels where substances are exchanged with cells. Blood leaving the heart reaches them only after passing through larger vessels.

questions.q: Which blood vessel carries blood towards the heart?
questions.explain: Veins carry blood from the organs and tissues back towards the heart.
questions.lo: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries

notes.1: Arteries carry blood in the other direction, away from the heart.
notes.2: Phloem is a tissue in plants that carries food. It is not a blood vessel.
notes.3: Capillaries are tiny vessels where substances are exchanged with cells. Blood collects from them into larger vessels before returning to the heart.

questions.q: Which blood vessel is the site of exchange of substances?
questions.explain: Capillaries have walls only one cell thick, so substances can pass between the blood and the body cells easily.
questions.lo: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries

notes.0: Veins have walls too thick for substances to pass through easily. Exchange happens in the smallest vessels, which have very thin walls.
notes.2: Phloem is a plant tissue that carries food. It is not a blood vessel.
notes.3: Arteries have thick, muscular walls. Exchange happens in the smallest vessels, which have very thin walls.

why.right: Exchange happens in capillaries because their walls are only one cell thick, so substances pass through easily.
wrong: Exchange happens in capillaries because their walls are thick and muscular, so they squeeze substances out.
Exchange happens in capillaries because their blood flows very fast, so substances are pushed out.

questions.q: Capillaries are suited to exchange because they have
questions.explain: Capillary walls are only one cell thick. Substances such as oxygen and digested food can pass through them quickly by diffusion.
questions.lo: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries

notes.0: Thick walls would slow down the movement of substances. For exchange, substances must cross the wall quickly.
notes.1: Capillaries are full of blood. The substances carried in this blood are what is exchanged with the cells.
notes.3: Only the heart acts as a pump. Capillaries are tubes, and exchange depends on how easily substances cross the wall.

why.right: Thin capillary walls help exchange because substances have only a short distance to diffuse through.
wrong: Thin capillary walls help exchange because they make the blood flow faster than in arteries.
Thin capillary walls help exchange because they let blood cells leave and enter the body cells.

questions.q: A blood vessel carries blood from the heart to the legs. What is it?
questions.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, so the vessel taking blood from the heart to the legs is an artery.
questions.lo: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries

notes.1: Capillaries are tiny vessels inside tissues where exchange happens. They do not carry blood the long distance away from the heart.
notes.2: Veins carry blood back towards the heart. This vessel carries blood in the opposite direction.

why.right: The vessel is an artery because arteries carry blood away from the heart to the organs.
wrong: The vessel is an artery because arteries carry blood only to the lower half of the body.
The vessel is an artery because arteries carry blood that has no oxygen left in it.

questions.q: A blood vessel carries blood from the arm back to the heart. What is it?
questions.explain: Veins carry blood back towards the heart, so the vessel taking blood from the arm to the heart is a vein.
questions.lo: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries

notes.0: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. This vessel carries blood in the opposite direction.
notes.2: Capillaries are tiny vessels inside tissues where exchange happens. Blood from them collects into larger vessels to return to the heart.

why.right: The vessel is a vein because veins carry blood from the organs back towards the heart.
wrong: The vessel is a vein because veins carry blood only in the arms and the upper body.
The vessel is a vein because veins carry blood that is rich in oxygen to the heart.

questions.q: Oxygen moves from a blood vessel into muscle cells. Which vessel is it?
questions.explain: Capillaries have walls only one cell thick. Oxygen diffuses through these walls from the blood into the muscle cells.
questions.lo: Describe the functions of arteries, veins and capillaries

notes.0: Arteries have thick walls, so oxygen cannot pass through them easily. Exchange with cells happens in the smallest vessels.
notes.2: Veins have walls too thick for easy exchange, and their blood has already given up much of its oxygen.

why.right: Oxygen reaches muscle cells through capillaries because capillary walls are only one cell thick.
wrong: Oxygen reaches muscle cells through capillaries because capillaries pump the oxygen into the cells.
Oxygen reaches muscle cells through capillaries because capillaries have the thickest walls of all vessels.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of blood flow from the heart?
questions.explain: Blood leaves the heart in arteries, passes through capillaries in the tissues, then returns to the heart in veins.
questions.lo: Trace the pathway of blood through the vessels and the content of the blood

notes.0: Veins return blood to the heart, so they come last. Blood must exchange substances with cells before it returns.
notes.1: Capillaries are inside the tissues. Blood leaving the heart reaches the tissues only after travelling in a larger vessel.
notes.2: Veins bring blood back to the heart. They are not the first vessels blood enters when it leaves the heart.

why.right: Blood flows in this order because arteries branch into capillaries, which then join up to form veins.
wrong: Blood flows in this order because the capillaries pump the blood from the arteries into the veins.
Blood flows in this order because the veins must collect oxygen before the blood reaches the capillaries.

questions.q: Blood in the veins of the body is
choices: poor in oxygen, rich in carbon dioxide
rich in oxygen, poor in carbon dioxide
poor in oxygen and carbon dioxide
rich in oxygen and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Body cells take oxygen from the blood and add carbon dioxide to it. Blood in the body's veins is poor in oxygen and rich in carbon dioxide.
questions.lo: Trace the pathway of blood through the vessels and the content of the blood

notes.1: This describes blood that has just come from the lungs. Think about what the body cells have done to the blood before it enters the veins.
notes.2: Cells take oxygen from the blood, but they also give something to it. Think about the waste gas made in respiration.
notes.3: Body cells use up oxygen as the blood passes them. Blood in the veins has already given oxygen away.

why.right: Blood in body veins is low in oxygen because the cells used its oxygen and added carbon dioxide.
wrong: Blood in body veins is low in oxygen because the thick vein walls let oxygen leak out.
Blood in body veins is low in oxygen because the heart removes oxygen before pumping it out.

questions.q: Blood has just left the capillaries in an arm. It now flows into a
questions.explain: Capillaries join together to form veins, which carry the blood back towards the heart.
questions.lo: Trace the pathway of blood through the vessels and the content of the blood

notes.0: Xylem is a transport tissue in plants. It is not part of the human transport system.
notes.1: Blood must return to the heart before it can be pumped to another part of the body such as a leg.
notes.3: Arteries carry blood away from the heart towards the capillaries. Blood leaving the capillaries goes the other way.

why.right: Blood leaving capillaries enters veins because capillaries join together to form veins that lead to the heart.
wrong: Blood leaving capillaries enters veins because veins carry blood away from the heart to the next organ.
Blood leaving capillaries enters veins because veins are the only vessels with walls thin enough to take it.

questions.q: Blood returns to the heart from the legs. Where is it pumped next?
questions.explain: Blood from the legs is low in oxygen. The heart pumps it to the lungs to take in oxygen and get rid of carbon dioxide.
questions.lo: Trace the pathway of blood through the vessels and the content of the blood

notes.0: The small intestine receives blood that has been pumped round the body. Blood returning from the legs first needs more oxygen.
notes.1: This blood has just come from the legs and is low in oxygen. It must gain oxygen before going back out to the body.
notes.2: The brain needs blood rich in oxygen. Blood returning from the legs is low in oxygen and must take in more first.

why.right: Blood from the legs goes to the lungs next because it is low in oxygen and must take in more.
wrong: Blood from the legs goes to the lungs next because the lungs are the closest organ to the legs.
Blood from the legs goes to the lungs next because the lungs digest the food that it carries.

questions.q: Arteries branch into smaller vessels near the cells. These smaller vessels are
questions.explain: Arteries branch into tiny capillaries near the cells. Capillary walls are thin enough for substances to be exchanged with the cells.
questions.lo: Trace the pathway of blood through the vessels and the content of the blood

notes.0: Veins carry blood back to the heart after it has passed the cells. They form when the smallest vessels join up.
notes.2: Phloem is a plant tissue that carries food. It is not a blood vessel.
notes.3: The new vessels are much smaller, with walls thin enough for exchange. They have a different name from the vessels they branch from.

why.right: Arteries branch into capillaries because cells need tiny thin-walled vessels close to them for exchange.
wrong: Arteries branch into capillaries because cells need thick-walled vessels close to them to push blood in.
Arteries branch into capillaries because blood must be cleaned of all germs before it reaches the veins.

questions.q: Multicellular organisms need a transport system to
choices: make all cells the same size
move substances quickly to all cells
questions.explain: In a large organism, diffusion alone is too slow to reach cells deep inside. A transport system moves substances quickly to all cells.
questions.lo: Explain the need for a transport system in multicellular organisms

notes.0: Cells in an organism differ in size and type. A transport system carries substances and does not change the size of cells.
notes.1: Diffusion still happens between the blood and the cells. A transport system works together with diffusion rather than stopping it.
notes.2: All cells still need food. A transport system delivers food, so it does not remove the need for it.

why.right: Large organisms need a transport system because diffusion alone is too slow to supply cells deep inside.
wrong: Large organisms need a transport system because their cells cannot take in any substances by diffusion.
Large organisms need a transport system because their inner cells make all the food the outer cells need.

questions.q: A large animal has no transport system. What would happen to its inner cells?
choices: they would die from lack of food
they would make their own oxygen
questions.explain: Without a transport system, food and oxygen would diffuse too slowly to reach the inner cells. These cells would not get enough and would die.
questions.lo: Explain the need for a transport system in multicellular organisms

notes.0: Inner cells are far from the surface. Substances would take too long to reach them by diffusion alone.
notes.1: Growth needs a good supply of food and oxygen. Inner cells far from the surface would get very little of either.
notes.3: Animal cells cannot make their own oxygen. They depend on oxygen brought to them from outside.

why.right: The inner cells would die because food and oxygen would diffuse too slowly to reach them.
wrong: The inner cells would die because the outer cells would take away all of their water.
The inner cells would die because carbon dioxide would diffuse into them from the air too quickly.

questions.q: What does the xylem transport?
questions.explain: Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots up to the stems and leaves.
questions.lo: State that the xylem transports water and mineral salts and the phloem transports food

notes.1: Blood is the transport liquid in animals. Plants do not have blood.
notes.2: Sugar is food made in the leaves. It is carried by the other transport tissue in plants.
notes.3: Gases enter and leave a plant mainly through tiny openings in the leaves, not through a transport tissue.

questions.q: What does the phloem transport?
questions.explain: Phloem carries food, such as sugar, made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.
questions.lo: State that the xylem transports water and mineral salts and the phloem transports food

notes.0: Oxygen moves into and out of the leaf through tiny openings by diffusion. Phloem does not carry it.
notes.2: Soil particles stay in the soil. Plants take in only water and dissolved substances from the soil.
notes.3: Water and mineral salts travel up from the roots in the other transport tissue of the plant.

questions.q: In which direction does the xylem transport substances?
questions.explain: Xylem carries water and mineral salts in one direction only, upwards from the roots to the leaves.
questions.lo: State that the xylem transports water and mineral salts and the phloem transports food

notes.0: Two-way transport happens in the other plant transport tissue, which moves food. Water travels only one way from where it is absorbed.
notes.1: Water is absorbed at the roots, which are at the bottom of the plant. It has to travel away from the roots to reach the leaves.
notes.3: Water travels from the roots to the leaves. The roots and the leaves are at different heights, not side by side.

why.right: Xylem carries water upwards only because water enters at the roots and is lost from the leaves.
wrong: Xylem carries water upwards only because water always flows towards the warmest part of the plant.
Xylem carries water upwards only because the leaves make the water that the roots need.

questions.q: Sugar made in a leaf reaches the roots. Which tissue carried it?
questions.explain: Phloem carries food, such as sugar, from the leaves to other parts of the plant, including the roots.
questions.lo: State that the xylem transports water and mineral salts and the phloem transports food

notes.1: Stomata are tiny openings in the leaf for gases. They do not carry substances through the plant.
notes.2: Xylem carries water and mineral salts upwards from the roots. Sugar travels in the other transport tissue.

why.right: The sugar was carried by phloem because phloem carries food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
wrong: The sugar was carried by phloem because phloem carries only substances that the roots absorbed from the soil.
The sugar was carried by phloem because phloem is the tissue that makes sugar inside the leaves.

questions.q: Mineral salts from the soil reach a flower bud. Which tissue carried them?
questions.explain: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots up to all parts of the plant, including flower buds.
questions.lo: State that the xylem transports water and mineral salts and the phloem transports food

notes.0: Phloem carries food made in the leaves. Substances taken in from the soil travel in the other transport tissue.
notes.1: Stomata are tiny openings in the leaf for gases. They do not carry substances through the plant.

why.right: The mineral salts were carried by xylem because xylem carries water and dissolved salts up from the roots.
wrong: The mineral salts were carried by xylem because xylem carries food made in the leaves to the flowers.
The mineral salts were carried by xylem because xylem takes in mineral salts from the air through the leaves.

questions.q: A ring of phloem is removed from a tree trunk. What stops reaching the roots?
questions.explain: Phloem carries sugar from the leaves down to the roots. Removing a ring of phloem stops sugar from reaching the roots.
questions.lo: State that the xylem transports water and mineral salts and the phloem transports food

notes.0: Water travels up from the roots in the xylem, which is left in place. Think about what moves down from the leaves.
notes.1: Mineral salts travel up from the roots in the xylem, which is left in place. Think about what moves down from the leaves.
notes.2: Roots take in oxygen directly from the air spaces in the soil. Oxygen does not travel to them through the trunk.

why.right: Sugar stops reaching the roots because sugar made in the leaves travels down to the roots in the phloem.
wrong: Sugar stops reaching the roots because sugar is made in the bark, and the bark has been removed.
Sugar stops reaching the roots because sugar travels up from the soil to the roots in the phloem.

questions.q: A celery stalk stands in red dye. Which tissue turns red first?
questions.explain: The red dye travels with the water up the xylem, so the xylem turns red first.
questions.lo: Infer from an investigation that the xylem transports water and mineral salts

notes.1: Stomata are tiny openings on the leaves, not inside the stalk. The dye travels up inside the stalk with the water.
notes.2: Celery has no bark. The dye moves with the water inside the stalk, in the tissue that carries water.
notes.3: Phloem carries food made in the leaves. The dye is in the water, so look for the tissue that carries water.

why.right: The xylem turns red because the dye moves up the stalk with the water that the xylem carries.
wrong: The xylem turns red because the dye moves down the stalk with the food that the xylem carries.
The xylem turns red because the dye is made into food inside the xylem cells of the stalk.

questions.q: A stalk stands in dyed water. Dye reaches the leaves. This shows the xylem
questions.explain: The dye moves up from the water to the leaves. This shows that the xylem transports water upwards.
questions.lo: Infer from an investigation that the xylem transports water and mineral salts

notes.0: Carbon dioxide enters a leaf through tiny openings. The dye experiment shows what moves up the stalk.
notes.2: Food is made in the leaves by photosynthesis. The xylem is a transport tissue, so it carries substances rather than making them.
notes.3: The dye started in the water at the bottom and moved up. Sugar is carried by the other transport tissue.

why.right: The dye reaches the leaves because it is dissolved in the water that the xylem carries up the stalk.
wrong: The dye reaches the leaves because it is dissolved in the sugar that the xylem carries up the stalk.
The dye reaches the leaves because the leaves absorb it from the air around the top of the stalk.

questions.q: Dyed water is added to the soil of a potted plant. Which tissue becomes stained?
questions.explain: The roots absorb the dyed water and the xylem carries it up the plant, so the xylem becomes stained.
questions.lo: Infer from an investigation that the xylem transports water and mineral salts

notes.0: Stomata are tiny openings in the leaves for gases. Water from the soil travels inside the roots and stem.
notes.1: Bark is the outer layer of a trunk. Water from the soil travels up in a tissue inside the stem.
notes.2: Phloem carries food made in the leaves. The dye is in the water, so look for the tissue that carries water.

why.right: The xylem is stained because the roots absorb the dyed water and the xylem carries it upwards.
wrong: The xylem is stained because the leaves absorb the dye and the xylem carries it downwards.
The xylem is stained because the dye mixes with the sugar that the xylem carries to the roots.

questions.q: A plant's xylem is blocked. What happens to its leaves?
questions.explain: Blocked xylem cannot carry water to the leaves. The leaves lose water that is not replaced, so they wilt.
questions.lo: Infer from an investigation that the xylem transports water and mineral salts

notes.0: Growth needs water. If the xylem is blocked, the leaves receive less water, not more.
notes.1: Leaves keep losing water through their stomata. If no water arrives to replace it, the leaves change.
notes.2: Photosynthesis needs water. With the xylem blocked, less water reaches the leaves, so less sugar can be made.

why.right: The leaves wilt because the water they lose is not replaced when water cannot travel up the xylem.
wrong: The leaves wilt because sugar cannot travel up the xylem from the roots to feed them.
The leaves wilt because carbon dioxide cannot travel up the xylem from the soil to the leaves.

questions.q: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of
questions.explain: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
questions.lo: Define diffusion and predict the direction of diffusion from concentrations

notes.0: Diffusion is not about water and soil. It describes particles moving between regions with different concentrations.
notes.2: This is the reverse of diffusion. Particles spread out from where they are crowded.
notes.3: When the concentration is equal everywhere, there is no net movement. Diffusion needs a difference in concentration.

questions.q: Region X has more oxygen than region Y. Which way does oxygen diffuse?
questions.explain: Oxygen diffuses from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated, so it moves from X to Y.
questions.lo: Define diffusion and predict the direction of diffusion from concentrations

notes.0: Oxygen particles move all the time. When one region has more oxygen, there is a net movement until the concentrations are equal.
notes.1: This direction is from lower to higher concentration. Diffusion goes from where there are more particles to where there are fewer.

why.right: Oxygen moves from X to Y because diffusion goes from a higher to a lower concentration.
wrong: Oxygen moves from X to Y because diffusion carries on until all the oxygen is in Y.
Oxygen moves from X to Y because oxygen particles in Y move faster than those in X.

questions.q: A body cell has more carbon dioxide than the blood. Carbon dioxide diffuses
choices: from the cell into the blood
from the blood into the cell
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide diffuses from higher to lower concentration, so it moves from the cell into the blood.
questions.lo: Define diffusion and predict the direction of diffusion from concentrations

notes.1: This direction is from lower to higher concentration. Diffusion goes from where there are more particles to where there are fewer.
notes.2: Particles are always moving. When the concentrations differ, there is a net movement until they become equal.

why.right: Carbon dioxide moves into the blood because it diffuses from a higher to a lower concentration.
wrong: Carbon dioxide moves into the blood because the heart pumps it out of the body cell.
Carbon dioxide moves into the blood because the cell turns it into oxygen for the blood.

questions.q: Oxygen diffuses from region P to region Q. Which region had more oxygen?
questions.explain: Oxygen diffuses from higher to lower concentration. Since it moved from P to Q, region P had more oxygen.
questions.lo: Define diffusion and predict the direction of diffusion from concentrations

notes.0: With equal concentrations there would be no net movement. The oxygen moved, so the concentrations were different.
notes.1: Diffusion goes from more particles to fewer particles. Think about which region the oxygen left.

why.right: Region P had more oxygen because diffusion moves particles from a higher to a lower concentration.
wrong: Region P had more oxygen because oxygen particles in P move while particles in Q stay still.
Region P had more oxygen because diffusion carries on until all the oxygen has left region P.

questions.q: A medicine patch on the skin works by diffusion. Where is the medicine more concentrated?
questions.explain: Diffusion moves the medicine from higher to lower concentration. The medicine enters the skin, so it is more concentrated in the patch.
questions.lo: Define diffusion and predict the direction of diffusion from concentrations

notes.1: With equal concentrations there would be no net movement. The patch works only if the medicine keeps moving into the skin.
notes.2: If the skin had more medicine, the medicine would diffuse out of the skin into the patch. Think about which way it needs to go.

why.right: The patch has more medicine because diffusion moves it from a higher to a lower concentration.
wrong: The patch has more medicine because diffusion carries on until all the medicine leaves the patch.
The patch has more medicine because the skin pumps the medicine in from the patch.

questions.q: Digested food moves from the capillaries into body cells by
questions.explain: Digested food is more concentrated in the blood than in the cells, so it diffuses through the thin capillary walls into the cells.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves substances between capillaries and body cells

notes.0: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules only. Digested food is not water.
notes.2: Churning is the mixing of food by the stomach. It does not happen between capillaries and cells.
notes.3: The heart pushes blood along the vessels. Substances cross the capillary wall on their own, from higher to lower concentration.

why.right: Digested food enters body cells because it is more concentrated in the blood than in the cells.
wrong: Digested food enters body cells because the heart pushes it through the walls of the capillaries.
Digested food enters body cells because water carries it into the cells by osmosis.

questions.q: Why does oxygen leave a capillary and enter muscle cells?
choices: oxygen is more concentrated in the cells
oxygen is more concentrated in the blood
questions.explain: Oxygen is more concentrated in the blood than in the muscle cells. It diffuses from the capillary into the cells.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves substances between capillaries and body cells

notes.0: Veins carry blood back to the heart. They do not push oxygen into cells.
notes.1: Cells do not pump oxygen in. Oxygen enters cells on its own, depending on where it is more concentrated.
notes.2: If oxygen were more concentrated in the cells, it would diffuse out of them. Muscle cells use up oxygen in respiration.

why.right: Oxygen enters muscle cells because the cells use it in respiration, so its concentration there stays low.
wrong: Oxygen enters muscle cells because the cells store it in large amounts, so its concentration there stays high.
Oxygen enters muscle cells because the heart pumps it straight through the capillary walls into them.

questions.q: Waste substances diffuse into the capillaries because they are more concentrated in the
questions.explain: Waste substances are made in the body cells, so they are more concentrated there. They diffuse from the cells into the capillaries.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves substances between capillaries and body cells

notes.1: If wastes were more concentrated in the blood, they would diffuse out of the blood. Think about where the wastes are made.
notes.2: Exchange with body cells does not happen in the arteries. Think about where the wastes are made.
notes.3: The heart is not next to every body cell. Think about where the wastes are made and which way they diffuse.

why.right: Wastes enter the capillaries because they are made in the body cells, so they are more concentrated there.
wrong: Wastes enter the capillaries because the blood pulls them out of the cells until none are left.
Wastes enter the capillaries because the heart pumps them out of the cells into the blood.

questions.q: As blood flows through a capillary in a muscle, its oxygen concentration
questions.explain: Oxygen diffuses out of the blood into the muscle cells as the blood flows along, so its oxygen concentration decreases.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves substances between capillaries and body cells

notes.0: Muscle cells use oxygen. Oxygen moves from the blood into the cells, not from the cells into the blood.
notes.1: Oxygen passes through the thin capillary walls. Some of it leaves the blood as the blood flows past the muscle cells.

why.right: Oxygen in the capillary blood falls because oxygen diffuses from the blood into the muscle cells.
wrong: Oxygen in the capillary blood falls because the blood itself turns the oxygen into carbon dioxide.
Oxygen in the capillary blood falls because the capillary walls absorb the oxygen and store it.

questions.q: Gases diffuse into and out of a leaf through tiny openings called
questions.explain: Stomata are tiny openings, mainly on the underside of the leaf. Gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen diffuse through them.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves gases and mineral salts into and out of plant cells

notes.0: Root cells are found in the roots, not the leaf. They take in water and mineral salts from the soil.
notes.1: Xylem is a transport tissue that carries water and mineral salts. It is not an opening to the air.
notes.2: Phloem is a transport tissue that carries food. It is not an opening to the air.

questions.q: During photosynthesis, which gas diffuses into the leaf?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf through the stomata.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves gases and mineral salts into and out of plant cells

notes.0: Oxygen is produced by photosynthesis, so it moves out of the leaf. Think about which gas the leaf uses up.
notes.2: Nitrogen is in the air but is not used in photosynthesis. Think about which gas the leaf uses up.
notes.3: Water vapour diffuses out of the leaf, not in. The water used in photosynthesis comes from the roots.

why.right: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf because photosynthesis uses it up, so less is inside than outside.
wrong: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf because respiration uses it up, so less is inside than outside.
Carbon dioxide enters the leaf because the xylem pulls it in from the air through the roots.

questions.q: During photosynthesis, oxygen diffuses out of a leaf because it is
questions.explain: Photosynthesis produces oxygen inside the leaf, so oxygen is more concentrated inside. It diffuses out through the stomata.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves gases and mineral salts into and out of plant cells

notes.1: Xylem carries water and mineral salts. It does not pump gases out of the leaf.
notes.2: Phloem carries food made in the leaf. Gases leave the leaf by diffusion through tiny openings.
notes.3: If oxygen were more concentrated outside, it would diffuse into the leaf. Think about where photosynthesis makes oxygen.

why.right: Oxygen leaves the leaf because photosynthesis makes it inside the leaf, so more is inside than outside.
wrong: Oxygen leaves the leaf because respiration makes it inside the leaf, so more is inside than outside.
Oxygen leaves the leaf because leaf cells never use oxygen at any time of the day or night.

questions.q: Before mineral salts can diffuse into a root cell, they must be
questions.explain: Mineral salts must be dissolved in water before they can diffuse into root cells.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves gases and mineral salts into and out of plant cells

notes.0: Solid particles cannot pass into the cells. Mineral salts have to be in a form that can spread through water.
notes.2: Sugar is made by photosynthesis in the leaves. Mineral salts are taken in as they are, not changed into sugar.
notes.3: Heating is not needed. Mineral salts diffuse into roots at the normal temperature of the soil.

why.right: Mineral salts must be dissolved because only dissolved particles can spread through water into the root cells.
wrong: Mineral salts must be dissolved because only dissolved particles can be turned into sugar by the root cells.
Mineral salts must be dissolved because only dissolved particles can be pumped upwards by the phloem.

questions.q: Root cells keep taking in mineral salts. Why?
choices: the phloem brings in more salts
the xylem carries the salts away
questions.explain: The xylem carries mineral salts away from the root cells. This keeps their concentration in the root cells low, so more salts keep diffusing in.
questions.lo: Explain how diffusion moves gases and mineral salts into and out of plant cells

notes.0: Phloem carries food made in the leaves. It does not bring mineral salts into the roots.
notes.1: Leaves cannot make mineral salts. Plants take mineral salts in from the soil.
notes.2: If the soil had no salts, there would be none to take in. Think about what happens to the salts after they enter the root.

why.right: Root cells keep taking in salts because the salts are carried away, keeping their concentration low in the root.
wrong: Root cells keep taking in salts because salts always diffuse from a lower to a higher concentration.
Root cells keep taking in salts because the leaves pull the salts down to the roots through the phloem.

questions.q: Water enters root cells from the soil by
questions.explain: Water moves from the soil into root cells by osmosis, across the partially permeable cell membrane.
questions.lo: State that osmosis allows water to be absorbed at the roots

notes.0: Stomata are openings in the leaves. Water from the soil enters through the roots.
notes.1: Phloem carries food made in the leaves. It does not take water in from the soil.
notes.3: Diffusion of mineral salts moves salts, not water. Water moves into the root by a different process across the membrane.

questions.q: Osmosis needs water molecules and a
questions.explain: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane.
questions.lo: State that osmosis allows water to be absorbed at the roots

notes.0: Phloem is a plant tissue that carries food. Osmosis happens across a thin layer around cells, not in a transport tissue.
notes.1: The cell wall lets most substances through freely. Osmosis needs a layer that lets some molecules through and not others.
notes.3: Osmosis is about water molecules moving. Solid salt particles cannot move through a membrane.

questions.q: A man lost at sea drinks seawater. Water leaves his body cells by
questions.explain: Seawater is very salty. Water moves out of the body cells into the saltier liquid around them by osmosis.
questions.lo: State that osmosis allows water to be absorbed at the roots

notes.0: Capillaries do not burst from drinking seawater. Water moves out of cells across their membranes.
notes.2: Diffusion of oxygen moves oxygen, not water. Think about how water molecules move across a membrane.
notes.3: The heart pumps blood along the vessels. It does not move water out of cells.

why.right: Water leaves the cells because it moves through the cell membrane towards the saltier liquid outside.
wrong: Water leaves the cells because it moves through the cell membrane towards the less salty liquid outside.
Water leaves the cells because salt particles push the water out through the cell wall.

questions.q: Drug abuse is using drugs in a way that
questions.explain: Drug abuse is the use of drugs in a way that harms a person's health.
questions.lo: Describe the harmful effects of drug abuse on the transport system and other systems

notes.1: Improving fitness is a benefit. Drug abuse is defined by the damage it causes.
notes.2: Treating an illness is a proper use of medicine. Drug abuse is not a proper use.
notes.3: Following a prescription is the correct way to use medicine. Drug abuse is using drugs in ways that are not proper.

questions.q: Which is an effect of drug abuse on the circulatory system?
questions.explain: Drug abuse can narrow blood vessels and raise blood pressure, which affects the circulatory system.
questions.lo: Describe the harmful effects of drug abuse on the transport system and other systems

notes.0: A stomach ulcer is a problem in the digestive system. The circulatory system is the heart, blood and blood vessels.
notes.1: Memory loss is a problem in the nervous system. The circulatory system is the heart, blood and blood vessels.
notes.2: Lung cancer is a problem in the respiratory system. The circulatory system is the heart, blood and blood vessels.

questions.q: A drug abuser has narrowed arteries. What is the result?
choices: reduced blood flow to the limbs
questions.explain: Narrowed arteries leave less space for blood to flow. Less blood reaches the limbs.
questions.lo: Describe the harmful effects of drug abuse on the transport system and other systems

notes.0: Narrow arteries make it harder for blood to flow, so the blood pressure goes up, not down.
notes.2: Narrowing affects the blood vessels. Think about how much blood can pass through a narrow tube.
notes.3: A narrower tube lets less liquid through, not more. Think about how much blood can pass a narrowed artery.

why.right: Less blood reaches the limbs because narrow arteries leave less space for the blood to flow through.
wrong: Less blood reaches the limbs because narrow arteries let the blood leak out through their walls.
Less blood reaches the limbs because narrow arteries carry the blood back towards the heart instead.

questions.q: A smoker develops lung cancer. Which body system is affected?
questions.explain: Lung cancer affects the lungs, which are part of the respiratory system.
questions.lo: Describe the harmful effects of drug abuse on the transport system and other systems

notes.0: The circulatory system is the heart, blood and blood vessels. Think about which system the lungs belong to.
notes.1: The digestive system breaks down and absorbs food. The lungs are not part of it.
notes.2: The nervous system is the brain, spinal cord and nerves. The lungs are not part of it.

why.right: Lung cancer affects the respiratory system because the lungs are the organs that take in air.
wrong: Lung cancer affects the respiratory system because the lungs pump blood around the body.
Lung cancer affects the respiratory system because the lungs send nerve messages to the body.

questions.q: A drug abuser has an irregular heartbeat. Which body system is affected?
questions.explain: The heart is part of the circulatory system. An irregular heartbeat is a problem of the circulatory system.
questions.lo: Describe the harmful effects of drug abuse on the transport system and other systems

notes.0: The nervous system is the brain, spinal cord and nerves. Think about which system the heart belongs to.
notes.1: The respiratory system takes in air through the lungs. The heart is not part of it.
notes.3: The digestive system breaks down and absorbs food. The heart is not part of it.

why.right: An irregular heartbeat affects the circulatory system because the heart pumps blood around the body.
wrong: An irregular heartbeat affects the circulatory system because the heart takes in air for breathing.
An irregular heartbeat affects the circulatory system because the heart controls thinking and memory.

questions.q: A drug abuser has slower reactions and memory loss. Which body system is affected?
questions.explain: Reactions and memory are controlled by the brain and nerves, which make up the nervous system.
questions.lo: Describe the harmful effects of drug abuse on the transport system and other systems

notes.1: The respiratory system takes in air through the lungs. It does not control reactions or memory.
notes.2: The circulatory system moves blood around the body. It does not control reactions or memory.
notes.3: The digestive system breaks down and absorbs food. It does not control reactions or memory.

why.right: Slow reactions and memory loss affect the nervous system because the brain controls thinking and responses.
wrong: Slow reactions and memory loss affect the nervous system because the heart controls thinking and responses.
Slow reactions and memory loss affect the nervous system because the lungs control thinking and responses.

questions.q: Second-hand smoke from cigarettes
questions.explain: Second-hand smoke is breathed in by people nearby. It contains harmful substances that also harm their health.
questions.lo: Describe the harmful effects of drug abuse on the transport system and other systems

notes.0: Cigarette smoke contains harmful substances. It damages the heart and blood vessels rather than improving them.
notes.1: Smoke spreads into the air around the smoker. Other people breathe it in too.
notes.2: People nearby breathe in the same smoke. The harmful substances in it affect them as well.

why.right: Second-hand smoke harms others because they breathe in the same harmful substances as the smoker.
wrong: Second-hand smoke harms others because the smoke changes into germs that spread between people.
Second-hand smoke harms others because it removes all of the oxygen from the air in the room.

questions.q: In an organ transplant, the person who gives the organ is the
questions.explain: The donor is the person who gives the organ.
questions.lo: Identify ethical issues in organ transplants

notes.1: The recipient is the person who receives the organ, not the one who gives it.
notes.2: A patient is someone receiving medical care. In a transplant this usually describes the person who receives the organ.
notes.3: The doctor carries out or manages the transplant. The doctor does not give the organ.

questions.q: In an organ transplant, the person who receives the organ is the
questions.explain: The recipient is the person who receives the organ.
questions.lo: Identify ethical issues in organ transplants

notes.0: A nurse cares for patients. The nurse does not receive the organ.
notes.2: The surgeon carries out the operation. The surgeon does not receive the organ.
notes.3: The donor is the person who gives the organ, not the one who receives it.

questions.q: "Is the donor making the decision willingly?" Which ethical principle is this?
questions.explain: Respect for persons means people make their own decisions freely. Asking whether the donor chose willingly is about respect for persons.
questions.lo: Identify ethical issues in organ transplants

notes.0: Justice is about fairness, such as how organs are shared out. This question is about the donor's own choice.
notes.1: Minimal harm and maximised benefits is about weighing risks against benefits. This question is about the donor's own choice.

why.right: This question concerns respect for persons because it asks whether the donor chose freely without pressure.
wrong: This question concerns respect for persons because it asks whether organs are shared out fairly.
This question concerns respect for persons because it asks whether the operation will cause harm.

questions.q: "Is the way organs are allocated fair?" Which ethical principle is this?
questions.explain: Justice is about fairness. Asking whether organs are allocated fairly is about justice.
questions.lo: Identify ethical issues in organ transplants

notes.0: Minimal harm and maximised benefits is about weighing risks against benefits. This question is about fairness.
notes.1: Respect for persons is about people making their own free choices. This question is about how organs are shared out.

why.right: This question concerns justice because it asks whether organs are shared out fairly among patients.
wrong: This question concerns justice because it asks whether the donor chose freely without pressure.
This question concerns justice because it asks whether the operation will help more than it harms.

questions.q: "Will the transplant improve the patient's quality of life?" Which ethical principle is this?
questions.explain: Minimal harm and maximised benefits is about weighing risks against benefits. Asking whether the transplant improves quality of life is about its benefits.
questions.lo: Identify ethical issues in organ transplants

notes.1: Justice is about fairness, such as how organs are shared out. This question is about the good the transplant will do.
notes.2: Respect for persons is about people making their own free choices. This question is about the good the transplant will do.

why.right: This question concerns minimal harm and maximised benefits because it asks how much good the transplant does.
wrong: This question concerns minimal harm and maximised benefits because it asks whether organs are shared fairly.
This question concerns minimal harm and maximised benefits because it asks whether the donor chose freely.

questions.q: Why do some countries use an opt-out scheme for organ donation?
choices: to make organs cheaper to buy
to reduce the supply of organs
to increase the supply of organs
questions.explain: In an opt-out scheme, everyone is counted as a donor unless they choose not to be. This increases the number of organs available for transplants.
questions.lo: Identify ethical issues in organ transplants

notes.0: Long waiting lists are a problem that these schemes try to solve. More donors means patients wait less.
notes.1: Selling organs is not allowed. An opt-out scheme is about the number of donors, not the price of organs.
notes.2: Countries want more organs for patients who need them. A scheme that reduced the supply would make the shortage worse.

why.right: An opt-out scheme raises the supply because people are counted as donors unless they choose to say no.
wrong: An opt-out scheme raises the supply because people must pay a fee to be removed from the donor list.
An opt-out scheme raises the supply because living people must give an organ whenever they are asked.
